title: Reading, Writing, and Rounding Whole Numbers

explanation: The decimal system uses 10 digits (0–9). Position determines value.
Commas separate groups of three digits: [[kw:units]], [[kw:thousands]], [[kw:millions]], [[kw:billions]], [[kw:trillions]].
Each group has a hundreds, tens, and ones place.
[[imp:Each place value is 10 times the place to its right.]]
Zeros are placeholders – they keep other digits in the correct spot.

formulaCard.title: Expanded Form
notes: Value of a digit = digit × place value.

visuals.title: Place-Value Chart
visuals.caption: Groups separated by commas. Leftmost group may have fewer than three digits.

blocks.title: 1. Place Value: The Decimal System

examples.prompt: In 82,537, what is the value of the 5?
examples.title: A – Find the value of a digit

steps: Commas split the number into hundreds/tens/ones groups.
Each group is read alone, then the group name is added.
Without commas it's easy to misread the size.
examples.title: B – Why commas?
examples.prompt: Explain to a partner why we use commas and group names.
examples.peerPrompt: Try reading a long number without commas.

confusionCorner.body: Never say 'and' when reading whole numbers – 'and' means the decimal point. [[imp:Read 105 as 'one hundred five'.]]
confusionCorner.title: Watch out!

teacherCues: Draw the place-value chart on the board. Ask: 'How much is a billion?'
Emphasize: Each place is 10× the place to its right.

questions.feedbackIfWrong: The 4 is in the tens place.
questions.prompt: In 2,048, the digit 4 is in the ___ place.

hints: Ten‑thousands is the second place from the right.

discoveryHook.scenario: A pet store sold 1,254 bags of cat food. The '1' means one thousand because of [[kw:place value]]. Every digit gets its meaning from where it sits.
A check for $1,254 must be written as 'One thousand two hundred fifty‑four'. The word 'and' is used **only** for the cents (the decimal part).

blocks.title: 2. Reading & Writing Whole Numbers

explanation: [[kw:Verbal form]] = words; [[kw:Numeric form]] = digits.
Reading: start left, read each group of three digits, say the group name (skip 'units'). Ignore all‑zero groups.
Hyphenate 21–99: 'twenty‑one'.
To write a verbal number in digits, use the place‑value chart – fill empty spots with zeros.
[[imp:No 'and' between whole numbers; 'and' marks the decimal.]]

visuals.caption: Use commas in numeric form only.
visuals.title: Verbal ↔ Numeric

examples.prompt: Write 'five hundred three thousand, twelve' in digits.
examples.title: A – Verbal to numeric

examples.prompt: Why should you never read 105 as 'one hundred and five'?
examples.peerPrompt: What does 'and' mean in the decimal system?
steps: The correct reading is 'one hundred five'.
examples.title: B – The 'and' rule
C – Read a number with zeros
steps: The zero in 080 isn't spoken; 007 becomes 'seven'.

teacherCues: Write a large number on the board and read it aloud, pointing to each group.
Remind students to hyphenate numbers like twenty‑one.

confusionCorner.body: Hyphenate 21–99: 'twenty‑one' not 'twenty one'. [[imp:No commas in verbal form.]]
confusionCorner.title: Watch out!

hints: Billion has 9 zeros after the first digit.
There are no million or thousand groups.
challengeCorner.prompt: Write 'seventeen billion, two hundred one' numerically.

questions.prompt: Which word must you NEVER use when reading a whole number?
'Seventy thousand, four hundred one' numerically is ___.
hints: The combined number is the answer.

discoveryHook.scenario: A cat food company reports sales of \$3.5 million. To use this number, convert it to 3,500,000. It's just dropping the decimal and adding zeros.

hints: Think of 5/100 of a trillion as 50 billion.

explanation: News often shows numbers like \$2.3 billion – a decimal part of a large word.
Two‑step conversion: [[imp:1. Drop the decimal point and insert a comma. 2. Add zeros so the leftmost digit ends in the word name (million, billion, etc.).]]
Number of zeros: 1 million = 6 zeros, 1 billion = 9 zeros, 1 trillion = 12 zeros.
[[note:Always add commas to separate groups.]]

visuals.title: Conversion Examples
visuals.caption: Drop decimal, add zeros to match the word.

blocks.title: 3. Converting Parts of Millions & Billions

examples.prompt: Write \$4.25 trillion as a whole number.
steps: Trillion = 12 zeros. Move the 4 to hundred‑trillions: 4,250,000,000,000.
examples.title: A – Convert \$4.25 trillion

steps: Drop decimal (08), add zeros until the 8 is in the hundred‑thousands place.
examples.title: B – Why \$0.8 million = 800,000
C – Tiny decimal of a billion

Walk through the steps: drop the decimal, insert commas and zeros.

confusionCorner.body: Don't just write '3.5 million' as 3,500 – that's too small. [[imp:Add the correct number of zeros.]]

questions.prompt: To round, look at the digit to the ___ of the target place.
questions.feedbackIfWrong: Look at the digit to the right.
hints: If it's 5 or more you round up.

explanation: Rounding approximates a number to a chosen place value.
Three steps: [[imp:1. Identify the rounding digit. 2. Look right: if 5 or more, round the digit up; else keep it. 3. Change all digits to the right to zeros.]]
If rounding up makes a 9, carry over to the next left place.
[[kw:Rounding all the way]] = rounding to the first digit (all others become zeros).

visuals.title: Rounding Examples
visuals.caption: Always check the digit to the right.

confusionCorner.body: When a 9 rounds up, carry to the next place. Example: 3,972 to nearest hundred: 9+1=10, write 0, carry 1 → 4,000. [[imp:Always check for carry-over.]]
confusionCorner.title: Watch out!

challengeCorner.prompt: Round 399,501 to the nearest hundred thousand.

teacherCues: Post the three rounding steps. Use a number line to show why 9,362 rounds to 9,400.
Drill: 'Look right – 5 or more, round up.'

discoveryHook.scenario: A customer asks the total pet food cost for three purchases. Use the [[kw:blueprint aid]] – a simple plan to break down any word problem.

visuals.title: Blueprint in Action
visuals.caption: Follow these steps for every word problem.

explanation: The blueprint aid is a three‑step method:
[[imp:1. Understand – list known and unknown.]] [[imp:2. Solve – do the math step‑by‑step.]] [[imp:3. Conclude – state the answer and check.]]
This prevents careless mistakes and keeps you organized.
Key words: [[kw:total]] → add, [[kw:difference]] → subtract, [[kw:each]] → multiply or divide.

challengeCorner.prompt: Use the blueprint: A shelter has 23 cats, 45 dogs, and 12 rabbits. Total pets?

questions.prompt: The first blueprint step is to ___ the problem.
hints: Read and list what you know.
It's the U in a three‑step U‑S‑C.

questions.prompt: What is the final step? (one word)

hints: It comes between understand and conclude.
questions.prompt: The math is done in the ___ step.

confusionCorner.body: Skipping the 'understand' step is the #1 cause of mistakes. [[imp:Always note the knowns and unknowns first.]]
confusionCorner.title: Watch out!

blocks.title: 5. Blueprint Aid for Word Problems

steps: Understand: Known = daily counts. Unknown = sum.
Conclude: 533 bags sold. Check by adding in reverse.
examples.prompt: A store sold 125, 210, and 198 bags on three days. Total?
examples.title: A – Find a total
B – Why the blueprint helps
steps: Understanding ensures you know exactly what's asked.
It stops you from using the wrong numbers or operation.
The conclude step makes you verify the answer.
examples.peerPrompt: What happens when you skip the 'understand' step?
examples.prompt: Explain to a classmate how the blueprint prevents errors.

teacherCues: Display the blueprint: Understand → Solve → Conclude.
Model with a real problem, writing each step.
